paragraphs: SECTION 13.5.

The rearing of children — that is, laying a foundation of sound health in body and mind for the rising generation — has rightly been insisted on as woman’s particular calling; so the ignorance that makes women unfit for it must be contrary to the order of things. And I maintain that their minds can take in much more, and ought to, or they will never become sensible mothers. Many men who attend to the breeding of horses and oversee the running of the stable would — what a strange want of sense and feeling! — think themselves degraded by paying any attention to the nursery. Yet how many children are downright murdered by the ignorance of women! And when children escape, and are destroyed neither by unnatural neglect nor by blind indulgence, how few are properly handled as far as the infant mind is concerned! So a child whose spirit has been allowed to grow unruly at home is sent to school to have it broken; and the methods used there, which must be used to keep a number of children in order, scatter the seeds of almost every vice in soil thus violently torn up.

I have sometimes compared the struggles of these poor children — who ought never to have felt restraint, and would not have, had they always been held in with an even hand — to the desperate plunging of a spirited filly I once watched being broken on a beach: its feet sank deeper and deeper into the sand each time it tried to throw its rider, until at last it sullenly gave in.

I have always found horses, an animal I am fond of, very manageable when treated with humanity and steadiness, so I doubt whether the violent methods used to break them do not do them real harm. I am certain, however, that a child should never be tamed by force in this way after it has unwisely been allowed to run wild; for every violation of justice and reason in the treatment of children weakens their reason. And children take on a character so early that, as experience leads me to conclude, the foundation of the moral character is laid before their seventh year — the period during which women are given sole charge of them. Afterwards it too often happens that half the business of education is to correct faults they would never have acquired if their mothers had had more understanding; and the correcting is very imperfectly done if it is done in haste.

One striking example of women’s folly must not be left out: the way they treat servants in front of children, letting the children suppose that servants ought to wait on them and put up with their whims. A child should always be made to receive help from a man or woman as a favour; and as their first lesson in independence, children should be taught in practice, by their mother’s example, not to demand that personal attendance which it is an insult to humanity to demand when one is in health. Instead of being encouraged to put on airs of self-importance, they should first be made to feel the natural equality of man through a sense of their own weakness. Yet how often have I heard with indignation servants being peremptorily called to put children to bed, and then sent away again and again because master or miss clung to mamma to stay up a little longer. With servants thus made to wait slavishly on the little idol, all those most disgusting whims that mark a spoiled child were put on display.

In short, to speak of the majority of mothers: they either leave their children entirely to the care of servants, or, because the children are theirs, treat them like little demigods — though I have always noticed that the women who idolize their children in this way seldom show ordinary humanity to servants, or feel the slightest tenderness for any children but their own.

It is, however, these exclusive affections, and a purely personal way of seeing things, both produced by ignorance, that keep women forever at a standstill as regards improvement. They lead many women to devote their lives to their children only to weaken the children’s bodies and spoil their tempers, and also to thwart any plan of education that a more rational father may adopt; for unless the mother agrees, the father who imposes restraint will always be regarded as a tyrant.

Yet a woman with a sound constitution may fulfil the duties of a mother and still keep her person scrupulously neat, help to support her family if necessary, or develop her mind by reading and by conversation with both sexes alike. For nature has ordered things so wisely that if women nursed their own children, they would preserve their own health, and there would be such an interval between births that we should seldom see a house full of babies. And if they followed a plan of conduct, instead of wasting their time chasing the fashionable whims of dress, the management of their household and children need not shut them out from literature, nor prevent them from devoting themselves to a science with that steady attention which strengthens the mind, or from practising one of the fine arts that cultivate taste.

But paying visits to show off finery, card playing and balls, not to mention the idle bustle of the morning’s trifling, draw women away from their duty, making them insignificant and making them pleasing — in the present sense of the word — to every man except their husband. For a round of pleasures in which the affections are not exercised cannot be said to develop the understanding, though it is mistakenly called seeing the world. Meanwhile the heart is made cold and averse to duty by such senseless socializing, which habit makes necessary even after it has ceased to amuse.

But until there is more equality in society, until ranks are mingled and women set free, we shall not see that dignified domestic happiness whose simple grandeur cannot be appreciated by ignorant or corrupted minds. Nor will the important task of education ever be properly begun until a woman’s person is no longer preferred to her mind. For it would be as sensible to expect corn from weeds, or figs from thistles, as to expect a foolish, ignorant woman to be a good mother.
SECTION 13.6.

Now that I am entering on my concluding reflections, there is no need to tell the discerning reader that the discussion of this subject consists merely in laying out a few simple principles and clearing away the rubbish that obscured them. But since not all readers are discerning, I must be allowed to add some explanatory remarks to bring the subject home to reason — to that sluggish reason which lazily accepts opinions on trust and stubbornly defends them to save itself the labour of thinking.

Moralists have unanimously agreed that unless virtue is nursed by liberty it will never reach its proper strength — and what they say of man I extend to mankind. I insist that in all cases morals must rest on unchanging principles, and that no being who obeys any authority but that of reason can be called rational or virtuous.

To make women truly useful members of society, I argue that they should be led, by having their understandings cultivated on a broad scale, to acquire a rational love of their country founded on knowledge; for it is obvious that we take little interest in what we do not understand. And to give this general knowledge its due importance, I have tried to show that private duties are never properly fulfilled unless the understanding enlarges the heart, and that public virtue is simply the sum of private virtue. But the distinctions established in society undermine both, beating out the solid gold of virtue until it becomes nothing but a tinsel covering for vice. For as long as wealth makes a man more respected than virtue does, wealth will be sought before virtue; and as long as women’s persons are caressed when a childish simper shows an absence of mind, the mind will lie fallow. Yet true voluptuousness must come from the mind — for what can equal the sensations produced by mutual affection supported by mutual respect? What are the cold or feverish caresses of appetite, compared with the modest overflowing of a pure heart and an exalted imagination, but sin embracing death? Yes, let me tell the libertine of fancy, when he despises understanding in woman, that the mind he disregards gives life to the ardent affection from which alone rapture, short-lived as it is, can flow! And let me tell him that without virtue a sexual attachment must die out, like a tallow candle guttering in its socket, leaving an intolerable disgust. To prove this, I need only observe that men who have wasted a great part of their lives with women, and have sought pleasure with them with an eager thirst, hold the lowest opinion of the sex. Virtue, true refiner of joy! If foolish men were to frighten you from the earth so as to give free rein to all their appetites without a check, some sensual fellow of taste would climb the heavens to invite you back, to give relish to pleasure!

That women at present are made foolish or vicious by ignorance is not, I think, to be disputed; and it seems at least a probable conclusion from this observation that the most beneficial effects for the improvement of mankind might be expected from a REVOLUTION in female manners. For since marriage has been called the parent of those endearing affections that draw man out of the brutal herd, the corrupting intercourse between the sexes that wealth, idleness and folly produce is more universally harmful to morality than all the other vices of mankind taken together. The most sacred duties are sacrificed to adulterous lust, because before marriage men, through promiscuous intimacy with women, learned to regard love as a selfish gratification — learned to separate it not only from esteem but even from the affection built merely on habit, which mixes a little humanity with it. Justice and friendship are also defied, and that purity of taste is corrupted which would naturally lead a man to prefer an unaffected display of affection to affected airs. But that noble simplicity of affection which dares to appear unadorned has few attractions for the libertine, though it is the charm that, by strengthening the marriage tie, secures for the children of a warmer passion the parental attention they need; for children will never be properly educated until friendship exists between their parents. Virtue flees from a house divided against itself — and a whole legion of devils take up residence there.

The affection of husbands and wives cannot be pure when they share so few feelings, and when there is so little trust at home, as must be the case when their pursuits are so different. The intimacy from which tenderness should flow will not, cannot, exist between the vicious.

Maintaining, therefore, that the distinction between the sexes on which men have so warmly insisted is arbitrary, I have dwelt on an observation that several sensible men with whom I have discussed the subject admitted to be well founded. It is simply this: the scant chastity found among men, and the resulting disregard of modesty, tend to degrade both sexes; and further, until modesty is universally respected, the modesty of women, so called, will often be merely the artful veil of wantonness instead of the natural reflection of purity.

I firmly believe that most female follies spring from the tyranny of man; and I have likewise tried repeatedly to prove that the cunning which I admit is at present part of their character is produced by oppression. Were not dissenters, for example, a class of people described, with strict truth, as cunning? And may I not lay some weight on this fact to prove that whenever any power but reason curbs the free spirit of man, dissimulation is practised and the various shifts of craft are naturally called forth? Great attention to decorum, carried to the point of scrupulousness, and all that childish fuss about trifles and self-important solemnity which Butler’s caricature of a dissenter calls to mind, shaped their persons as well as their minds in the mould of prim littleness. I speak of them as a body, for I know how many ornaments of human nature have been numbered among the sectaries; yet I assert that the same narrow prejudice in favour of their sect that women have for their families prevailed in the dissenting part of the community, however worthy in other respects, and also that the same timid prudence, or the same headstrong efforts, often disgraced the endeavours of both. Oppression thus formed many features of their character to coincide exactly with that of the oppressed half of mankind. For is it not notorious that dissenters, like women, were fond of deliberating together and asking one another’s advice, until by a web of little contrivances some little end was achieved? A similar concern to preserve their reputation was conspicuous in the dissenting world and the female world, and it was produced by a similar cause.

In asserting the rights that women, in common with men, ought to fight for, I have not tried to excuse their faults, but to prove that those faults are the natural consequence of their education and position in society. If so, it is reasonable to suppose that they will change their character, and correct their vices and follies, once they are allowed to be free in a physical, moral and civil sense.

Let woman share the rights, and she will emulate the virtues of man; for once emancipated she must grow more perfect — or else justify the authority that chains so weak a being to her duty. If it is the latter, it will be expedient to open a new trade with Russia for whips: a present a father should always give his son-in-law on his wedding day, so that a husband may keep his whole family in order by the same means, and, without any violation of justice, reign wielding this sceptre as sole master of his house, because he is the only being in it who has reason — the divine, indefeasible, earthly sovereignty breathed into man by the Master of the universe. If this position is granted, women have no inherent rights to claim; and by the same rule their duties vanish, for rights and duties are inseparable.

Be just, then, O you men of understanding! Do not judge what women do wrong more severely than the vicious tricks of the horse or the ass for which you provide fodder; and allow the privileges of ignorance to her to whom you deny the rights of reason — or you will be worse than Egyptian taskmasters, expecting virtue where nature has not given understanding!
